questions.q: What is the main effect of increasing a tokenizer's vocabulary size on sequence length for a fixed piece of text?
options: Sequence length increases, since more tokens are needed
Sequence length tends to decrease, since more whole words get their own single token
Sequence length is unaffected by vocabulary size
Sequence length becomes random and unpredictable
questions.explain: A larger vocabulary lets more whole words (and common multi-word chunks) be represented as a single token, so the same text tokenizes into fewer tokens on average, shortening the sequence.

questions.q: How does vocabulary size affect a model's total parameter count?
options: It has no effect, since embeddings are computed on the fly and not stored
The embedding and output (unembedding) matrices scale linearly with vocab_size times hidden_size
Vocabulary size only affects the number of attention heads
Larger vocabularies always reduce the total parameter count
questions.explain: Every vocabulary entry needs a row in both the input embedding matrix and the output projection matrix, so total embedding-related parameters scale linearly with vocab_size times hidden_size.

questions.q: Why might rare tokens in a very large vocabulary end up 'undertrained'?
options: Rare tokens are automatically removed from the vocabulary during training
Rare tokens appear infrequently in the training corpus, so their embeddings receive fewer gradient updates than common tokens
Rare tokens require a different loss function than common tokens
Rare tokens can only be used during evaluation, never during training
questions.explain: Tokens that appear rarely in the corpus get fewer opportunities for gradient updates, so their learned representations can lag behind frequently-seen tokens -- a quality cost of larger vocabularies.

questions.q: Why do multilingual model families generally use larger vocabularies than English-only models?
options: Larger vocabularies make training faster for every language
Without broader vocabulary coverage, non-English text falls back to inefficient byte-level fragments, inflating token counts for those languages
Multilingual models cannot use byte-level BPE at all
Vocabulary size has no relationship to language coverage
questions.explain: A tokenizer trained mostly on English represents other languages inefficiently, needing many more small tokens per word. A larger, more balanced vocabulary gives other languages reasonably efficient whole-word or subword tokens too.

questions.q: Which of these vocabulary sizes is closest to GPT-2's actual tokenizer vocabulary size?
options: ~500 tokens
~5,000 tokens
~50,257 tokens
questions.explain: GPT-2's tokenizer uses a vocabulary of 50,257 tokens, a commonly cited reference point when calibrating vocabulary size choices.
